name: Deverbal Adjective in -able
pattern: Adj[verb base + -able], with related forms in -ible

entry.name: Deverbal Adjective in -able
entry.pattern: Adj[verb base + -able], with related forms in -ible

1.definition: Characterizes a potential participant of an action by the possibility or suitability of that action.
1.details: Readable normally describes what people can read. The productive transitive pattern is therefore oriented to the base verb’s object. A prepositional verb can supply an oblique participant, as in dependable. Intransitive-base and lexicalized readings, such as perishable, extend beyond the central pattern.

examples.note: Constructed example. The document is what one can search.

examples.form: A [dependable] source is hard to find.
examples.note: Constructed example with depend on as the relevant verb and preposition.

relatedConstructions.notes: The central reading is typically paraphrasable with a modal passive.
Washable and This fabric washes well can describe suitability for washing. One derives an adjective and the other forms a clause with an active verb.

grounds.note: Documents base types, modal interpretation and participant contrasts.

projection.target: For a new transparent formation with a transitive base, the default referent is what can undergo the action. Prepositional verbs can supply a different participant.
projection.evidence: CASA registers the -able and -ible family. CGEL describes the productive modal use and records prefixed, oblique and other departures from it.

curious.title: Adjectives ending in -able
curious.summary: In its central pattern, adding -able to a verb gives an adjective that says something can have that action done to it.
curious.body:
Searchable describes a document that someone can search. Readable normally describes what people can read. So a new -able adjective built on a verb that takes an object normally describes the thing the action would be done to, not the person doing it. There are related forms in -ible.

Some verbs bring a small word along. Dependable is built on depend on, and it describes what you can depend on.

Not every case fits. Perishable doesn't simply mean that something can be perished, so some -able words go beyond this central meaning.

examples.text: A [dependable] source is hard to find.

curious.try: Take a verb you use and add -able. Does the new word describe the thing the action would happen to?

teacher.summary: Helps explain that an -able adjective built on a transitive verb is oriented to the verb's object, and that its central reading can be paraphrased as can be Xed.
teacher.explain: A deverbal adjective in -able (or -ible) characterizes a potential participant of an action by the possibility or suitability of that action. With a transitive base the adjective is oriented to the base verb's object: readable describes what people can read. The central reading can typically be paraphrased with a modal passive (can be searched). A prepositional verb can supply an oblique participant, as in dependable (depend on). Intransitive-base and lexicalized readings, such as perishable, extend beyond this central pattern.
teacher.terms: The paraphrase can be called a modal passive.

examples.text: A [dependable] source is hard to find.

contrasts.note: A related idea in a clause with an active verb; washable is the adjective counterpart.

watch_for: A learner might read dependable as describing the person who depends, when it describes what can be depended on.
A learner might assume every -able word means can be Xed, though perishable and other lexicalized forms extend beyond that pattern.
teacher.activity: Students list verbs from a class text, add -able where it makes a word they know, and paraphrase each as can be Xed. They flag any word that doesn't paraphrase that way.

checked.note: Fixed: curious summary and body and teacher summary now confine object orientation to the central (transitive-base) pattern, as the entry does, and mention readings that go beyond it; dropped the claim that some -able words 'drifted' from the central meaning; dropped the unsupported 'verbal adjectives' traditional-term mapping.
